primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Type 2 diabetes develops when cells in muscle, fat, and liver do not respond well to insulin and the pancreas cannot produce enough insulin to maintain normal blood glucose.
vignette: A 48-year-old man with central obesity has polyuria and fasting hyperglycemia. Testing shows that his skeletal muscle and adipose cells respond poorly to insulin.
lead: Which pathophysiologic abnormality most directly characterizes the early disease?
distractors: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells
Failure of ADH release from the posterior pituitary
Excessive renal glucose reabsorption as the primary defect
distractor_notes: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells does not match NIDDK's defining type 2 pattern of poor tissue response to insulin.
Absolute absence of glucagon secretion does not match the demonstrated poor response of insulin-sensitive tissues to insulin.
Failure of antidiuretic hormone release does not explain the demonstrated insulin resistance with hyperglycemia.
Excessive renal glucose reabsorption does not explain the demonstrated poor response of muscle and adipose cells to insulin.
key_expl: NIDDK defines insulin resistance as poor response to insulin in muscle, fat, and liver cells; this is a central abnormality in type 2 diabetes.
objective: Explain type 2 diabetes through insulin resistance in insulin-sensitive tissues with inadequate pancreatic compensation.
clues: poor insulin response in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue

sources.title: Symptoms & Causes of Diabetes
sources.support: NIDDK states that type 2 diabetes develops when the body has trouble using insulin and the pancreas cannot produce enough to compensate; muscle, fat, and liver cells respond poorly to insulin.

sources.title: Type 2 Diabetes
sources.support: NIDDK describes insulin resistance and inadequate insulin production as central mechanisms of type 2 diabetes.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Abnormal embryonic migration of GnRH-producing neurons and olfactory neurons leads to hypogonadotropic hypogonadism together with anosmia or hyposmia.
vignette: A 17-year-old boy has absent pubertal development, small testes, low testosterone, low LH and FSH, and inability to smell coffee or peppermint. MRI shows hypoplastic olfactory bulbs.
lead: Which developmental process is most likely abnormal?
correct: Migration of GnRH-producing and olfactory neurons
distractors: Migration of neural crest cells into the adrenal medulla only
Descent of the testes through the inguinal canal
distractor_notes: Adrenal neural-crest migration does not explain anosmia plus hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.
Cryptorchidism can accompany hypogonadism but testicular descent is not the central defect producing absent GnRH and anosmia.
Müllerian fusion abnormalities affect female reproductive anatomy.
Pancreatic beta-cell differentiation affects insulin production, not puberty and olfaction.
key_expl: Kallmann syndrome results when olfactory and GnRH neurons fail to migrate normally during development, producing anosmia and deficient hypothalamic GnRH secretion.
objective: Link anosmia plus hypogonadotropic hypogonadism to failed embryonic neuronal migration.

sources.title: Kallmann syndrome
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes Kallmann syndrome as hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with impaired smell due to abnormal development/migration of olfactory and GnRH-related neurons.

sources.title: ANOS1 gene
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics explains ANOS1 involvement in migration of olfactory neurons and GnRH-producing neurons from the developing nose to the brain.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Germline loss-of-function variants in MEN1 reduce menin tumor-suppressor activity; a second somatic hit in susceptible endocrine cells permits tumor formation, especially in parathyroid, pituitary, and pancreatic endocrine tissue.
vignette: A 35-year-old woman has recurrent nephrolithiasis from primary hyperparathyroidism, a prolactinoma, and a pancreatic gastrinoma. Her father had similar endocrine tumors.
lead: Which gene class is most directly involved?
correct: Tumor-suppressor gene requiring loss of remaining normal function in tumor cells
distractors: Constitutively activating receptor tyrosine kinase only
Ion channel gene causing prolonged repolarization
distractor_notes: Activating RET mutations are characteristic of MEN2, not MEN1.
Mitochondrial tRNA mutations cause mitochondrial disorders rather than the MEN1 tumor pattern.
Ion-channel defects cause channelopathies such as long-QT syndromes.
Collagen mutations cause connective-tissue disorders rather than endocrine neoplasia.
key_expl: MEN1 encodes menin, a tumor suppressor; inherited loss of one copy followed by loss of the remaining functional copy permits endocrine tumor development.
objective: Explain MEN1 tumor formation using tumor-suppressor two-hit biology.

sources.title: Multiple endocrine neoplasia
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes MEN1 tumors in parathyroid, pituitary, and pancreas and explains autosomal dominant inheritance with a second somatic MEN1 hit in tumor cells.

sources.title: MEN1 gene
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes menin as a tumor suppressor and loss of both functional MEN1 copies in endocrine tumor cells.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Severe decompensated thyrotoxicosis, often triggered by infection or another major stressor in uncontrolled hyperthyroidism, causes extreme adrenergic/metabolic manifestations and multiorgan dysfunction.
vignette: A 42-year-old woman with untreated Graves disease develops pneumonia and then becomes febrile to 40.2°C, agitated, delirious, tachycardic at 165/min, and hypotensive with diarrhea.
distractor_notes: Myxedema coma is severe hypothyroidism with hypothermia, bradycardia, and depressed mental status.
Pheochromocytoma can cause adrenergic symptoms but does not explain severe decompensation in known uncontrolled Graves disease with very high temperature and thyrotoxic features.
Serotonin syndrome requires serotonergic drug exposure and typically includes neuromuscular hyperactivity such as clonus.
Sepsis may trigger thyroid storm, but the known uncontrolled hyperthyroidism plus extreme thyrotoxic manifestations identify thyroid storm as the integrated diagnosis.
key_expl: Thyroid storm is life-threatening worsening of uncontrolled hyperthyroidism, often precipitated by infection or other major stress.
objective: Recognize thyroid storm as decompensated severe thyrotoxicosis triggered by physiologic stress.
clues: infection followed by fever, delirium, extreme tachycardia

sources.title: Thyroid storm
sources.support: MedlinePlus describes thyroid storm as life-threatening severe thyrotoxicosis in uncontrolled hyperthyroidism, often triggered by infection, trauma, or other stress.

sources.title: Hyperthyroidism
sources.support: MedlinePlus identifies thyroid storm as a sudden severe worsening of hyperthyroidism with fever, altered alertness, cardiovascular complications, and need for emergency care.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Autoimmune thyroid inflammation during the first postpartum year causes leakage of stored thyroid hormone, often producing a transient hyperthyroid phase followed by temporary or persistent hypothyroidism.
vignette: A woman 3 months after delivery develops palpitations and heat intolerance with low TSH and elevated free T4. Two months later she develops fatigue, cold intolerance, high TSH, and low free T4. She has no thyroid pain.
lead: Which mechanism best explains this biphasic pattern?
correct: Autoimmune thyroid inflammation causing release of stored hormone followed by glandular hypofunction
distractors: Continuous autonomous thyroid-hormone synthesis from a toxic adenoma
Exogenous thyroid hormone ingestion followed by adrenal failure
Constitutive activation of the TSH receptor throughout both phases
distractor_notes: A toxic adenoma causes persistent autonomous hyperthyroidism rather than a hyper-to-hypothyroid sequence.
A TSH-secreting pituitary tumor would produce inappropriately high TSH during hyperthyroidism.
Exogenous hormone does not explain the characteristic postpartum inflammatory sequence.
TSH-receptor activation in Graves disease drives sustained hormone synthesis rather than inflammatory leakage followed by reduced function.
key_expl: Postpartum thyroiditis is autoimmune inflammation causing stored hormone leakage, transient hyperthyroidism, and often a subsequent hypothyroid phase.
objective: Explain the biphasic thyroid pattern after childbirth through postpartum autoimmune thyroiditis.
clues: hyperthyroid phase followed by hypothyroid phase

sources.title: Thyroid Disease & Pregnancy
sources.support: NIDDK describes postpartum thyroiditis as autoimmune thyroid inflammation in the first year after delivery, with hormone leakage causing hyperthyroidism followed in some women by hypothyroidism.

sources.title: Thyroiditis
sources.support: MedlinePlus provides official thyroid-disease context including inflammatory causes of changing thyroid function.

outline: Congenital hypothyroidism due to thyroid dyshormonogenesis
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Congenital hypothyroidism due to thyroid dyshormonogenesis
mechanism: Defects in thyroid-hormone synthesis enzymes such as thyroid peroxidase impair iodination of thyroglobulin, reducing thyroid hormone production and risking abnormal growth and neurodevelopment.
vignette: A newborn screening test shows markedly elevated TSH and low T4. The infant has an enlarged thyroid gland. Genetic testing reveals biallelic pathogenic variants in TPO.
correct: Iodination of thyroglobulin during thyroid hormone synthesis
distractors: Conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II
distractor_notes: Androgen-to-estrogen conversion requires aromatase, not TPO.
ACTH production is a pituitary process unrelated to thyroid peroxidase.
Angiotensin conversion uses ACE.
GLUT4 mediates insulin-responsive glucose uptake.
key_expl: Thyroid peroxidase catalyzes iodination reactions on thyroglobulin; loss of TPO function causes thyroid dyshormonogenesis and congenital hypothyroidism.
objective: Link TPO deficiency to impaired iodination and congenital thyroid-hormone deficiency.
clues: newborn high TSH/low T4 with goiter

sources.title: TPO gene
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics states that thyroid peroxidase adds iodine to thyroglobulin, a critical step in thyroid-hormone production, and that TPO variants can cause congenital hypothyroidism.

sources.title: Congenital hypothyroidism
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes thyroid dyshormonogenesis from TPO and other thyroid-hormone-synthesis genes and the developmental consequences of low thyroid hormone.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Loss of CYP19A1 aromatase activity prevents conversion of androgens to estrogens, raising androgen levels and lowering estrogen; placental aromatase deficiency can virilize a 46,XX fetus and cause maternal virilization during pregnancy.
vignette: A 46,XX newborn has ambiguous external genitalia but normal ovaries and uterus. During pregnancy, the mother developed new hirsutism and deepening of the voice that improves after delivery.
lead: Which enzymatic reaction is most likely impaired?
distractor_notes: Testosterone-to-DHT conversion requires 5-alpha-reductase and affects male external genital development.
Cholesterol side-chain cleavage is an early steroidogenesis step and would reduce multiple steroid classes.
17-alpha/21-hydroxylase pathway defects cause congenital adrenal hyperplasia patterns rather than isolated aromatase deficiency.
PNMT converts norepinephrine to epinephrine in adrenal medulla.
key_expl: Aromatase converts androgens to estrogens; placental aromatase deficiency increases androgen exposure to both a 46,XX fetus and the pregnant mother.
objective: Explain virilization in aromatase deficiency through failure of androgen-to-estrogen conversion.
clues: 46,XX infant with ambiguous genitalia and normal internal female organs

sources.title: Aromatase deficiency
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes CYP19A1 deficiency, reduced estrogen, increased androgens, virilization of affected 46,XX fetuses, and maternal virilization during pregnancy.

sources.title: CYP19A1 gene
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics states that aromatase converts androgens to estrogens, including in the placenta during fetal development.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Loss-of-function CASR variants reduce calcium-sensing receptor activity, so parathyroid and renal cells perceive extracellular calcium as lower than it is, producing mild hypercalcemia with inappropriately low urinary calcium.
vignette: A 31-year-old woman is found incidentally to have serum calcium of 11.1 mg/dL. PTH is normal-high. Twenty-four-hour urine calcium is very low. Her father and sister have similar lifelong findings without kidney stones.
lead: Which molecular defect is most likely?
distractors: Loss of vitamin D receptor function
distractor_notes: RET activation causes MEN2 syndromes.
MEN1 loss predisposes to endocrine tumors and hyperparathyroidism but does not characteristically cause lifelong hypocalciuric hypercalcemia across relatives.
TSH receptor activation causes autonomous hyperthyroidism.
Vitamin D receptor defects cause vitamin D–resistant rickets and disturbed bone/mineral metabolism rather than classic FHH.
key_expl: FHH is caused by reduced CaSR signaling and is characterized by mild hypercalcemia with low urinary calcium excretion.
objective: Differentiate FHH from primary hyperparathyroidism using hypocalciuria and CASR biology.

sources.title: CASR gene
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics states that loss-of-function CaSR variants can cause familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia with hypercalcemia and low urinary calcium.

sources.title: Calcium Blood Test
sources.support: MedlinePlus provides official context for calcium regulation by parathyroid hormone, vitamin D, kidneys, and bone.

outline: Cervical cancer driven by persistent high-risk HPV
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Cervical cancer driven by persistent high-risk HPV
mechanism: Persistent infection with high-risk HPV, especially types 16 and 18, disrupts normal control of cervical-cell growth and can progress through precancerous lesions to invasive cervical cancer.
vignette: A 43-year-old woman with years of missed screening has postcoital bleeding. Cervical biopsy shows invasive squamous cell carcinoma, and tumor testing detects high-risk HPV type 16.
lead: Which etiologic factor most directly caused the malignant transformation?
correct: Persistent infection with high-risk human papillomavirus
distractor_notes: Hepatitis A does not cause cervical carcinoma.
H. pylori is linked to gastric disease and certain gastric lymphomas/carcinomas, not cervical cancer.
EBV contributes to several lymphoid and epithelial cancers but is not the dominant cause of cervical cancer.
CFTR dysfunction causes cystic fibrosis.
key_expl: Virtually all cervical cancers are caused by persistent high-risk HPV infection, particularly HPV 16 and 18.
objective: Link persistent high-risk HPV infection to cervical carcinogenesis.
clues: HPV16 detected with poor screening history

sources.title: Cervical Cancer Causes, Risk Factors, and Prevention
sources.support: NCI states that persistent infection with high-risk HPV causes virtually all cervical cancers and identifies HPV16/18 as major causal types.

sources.title: HPV and Cancer
sources.support: NCI explains how long-lasting high-risk HPV infection alters cervical cells and can progress from precancer to cancer.

primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Ascending infection of the upper female genital tract causes endometritis/salpingitis; gonorrhea and chlamydia are common causes, and tubal inflammation/scarring can lead to infertility and ectopic pregnancy.
vignette: A 21-year-old sexually active woman has lower abdominal pain, fever, mucopurulent cervical discharge, and marked cervical-motion tenderness. Pregnancy test is negative.
distractor_notes: Cystitis causes urinary symptoms and does not typically produce cervical-motion tenderness and mucopurulent discharge.
Ectopic pregnancy must be excluded clinically, but a negative pregnancy test plus fever and cervical inflammatory findings favor PID.
Appendicitis does not cause mucopurulent cervicitis or cervical-motion tenderness as a defining feature.
Endometriosis causes chronic/cyclic pelvic pain rather than febrile ascending infection with purulent cervical discharge.
key_expl: Lower abdominal pain with cervical-motion tenderness in an STI-risk patient is a classic clinical pattern for PID.
objective: Recognize PID clinically and distinguish it from other causes of pelvic pain.

sources.title: About Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID)
sources.support: CDC defines PID as infection of female reproductive organs often caused by untreated STIs such as gonorrhea or chlamydia and notes infertility risk.

sources.title: Pelvic Inflammatory Disease - STI Treatment Guidelines
sources.support: CDC recommends presumptive PID treatment in at-risk women with pelvic pain and cervical-motion, uterine, or adnexal tenderness.

outline: Tubal-factor infertility after gonococcal pelvic inflammatory disease
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Tubal-factor infertility after gonococcal pelvic inflammatory disease
mechanism: Untreated gonococcal infection can ascend to cause PID; inflammatory injury and scarring of fallopian tubes can obstruct gamete transport and cause infertility.
vignette: A 29-year-old woman has been unable to conceive for 18 months. Hysterosalpingography shows bilateral tubal occlusion. She had two episodes of untreated gonorrhea-associated PID in her early twenties.
lead: Which mechanism most likely caused her infertility?
correct: Inflammatory scarring and obstruction of the fallopian tubes
distractors: Loss of ovarian follicles before age 40
distractor_notes: GnRH deficiency causes hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, not bilateral tubal occlusion.
Primary ovarian insufficiency causes follicular dysfunction and elevated gonadotropins rather than scarred tubes.
Androgen-receptor defects affect sexual development, not acquired tubal scarring.
Endometrial progesterone resistance does not explain bilateral tubal occlusion after PID.
key_expl: Repeated PID can scar fallopian tubes; CDC notes gonorrhea/chlamydia-associated PID as an important cause of infertility.
objective: Explain post-PID infertility through fallopian-tube inflammation and scarring.

sources.title: About Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID)
sources.support: CDC states that untreated gonorrhea and chlamydia can cause PID and that women with PID may have difficulty becoming pregnant.

sources.title: Pelvic Inflammatory Disease - STI Treatment Guidelines
sources.support: CDC describes PID-associated reproductive tract damage and infertility risk, including from mild or unrecognized PID.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Treponema pallidum can cross the placenta during maternal infection and infect the fetus; untreated maternal syphilis can cause fetal loss, prematurity, rash, hepatosplenomegaly, bone disease, and neurologic injury.
vignette: A newborn has hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, anemia, and a diffuse rash involving the palms and soles. The mother had untreated syphilis during pregnancy.
lead: Which route of acquisition is most likely?
distractors: Reactivation of a latent neonatal herpesvirus
distractor_notes: Congenital syphilis is acquired from maternal infection during pregnancy, not by fecal-oral spread.
Respiratory droplets are not the mechanism of fetal syphilis infection.
Syphilis is not mosquito-borne.
The syndrome is due to Treponema pallidum acquired from the mother, not latent herpesvirus reactivation.
key_expl: Congenital syphilis occurs when maternal syphilis is transmitted to the fetus during pregnancy.
objective: Recognize congenital syphilis and its transplacental route of fetal infection.

sources.title: About Congenital Syphilis
sources.support: CDC states that congenital syphilis occurs when syphilis passes to a baby during pregnancy and describes rash, anemia, hepatosplenomegaly, bone and neurologic complications.

sources.title: Syphilis During Pregnancy - STI Treatment Guidelines
sources.support: CDC describes fetal infection risk during maternal syphilis and the importance of penicillin treatment during pregnancy.

primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Loss or dysfunction of ovarian follicles before age 40 lowers estrogen and ovarian inhibin output, reducing negative feedback and producing elevated gonadotropins, especially FSH, with irregular or absent menses and infertility.
vignette: A 34-year-old woman has 8 months of irregular menses, hot flashes, vaginal dryness, and infertility. Pregnancy test is negative. Estradiol is low and FSH is repeatedly elevated.
lead: Which endocrine pattern best explains these findings?
correct: Ovarian follicular failure with loss of negative feedback on pituitary gonadotropins
distractors: Hypothalamic GnRH deficiency with low FSH and LH
Constitutive ovarian androgen production with preserved follicle reserve
distractor_notes: Hypothalamic GnRH deficiency produces low or inappropriately normal gonadotropins.
Pituitary failure similarly lowers FSH/LH rather than raising FSH.
Hyperprolactinemia suppresses GnRH and typically lowers gonadotropins.
Androgen excess such as PCOS does not produce the classic low-estrogen/high-FSH follicular-failure pattern.
key_expl: POI is reduced ovarian function before age 40; loss of ovarian follicular function lowers estrogen and permits FSH to rise.
objective: Recognize primary ovarian insufficiency from age under 40, menstrual irregularity, low estrogen, and elevated FSH.

sources.title: Primary Ovarian Insufficiency
sources.support: MedlinePlus defines POI as ovarian dysfunction before age 40, describes irregular or missed periods and infertility, and explains follicular depletion/dysfunction.

sources.title: Fragile X-associated primary ovarian insufficiency
sources.support: MedlinePlus Genetics describes POI with reduced ovarian function, irregular/absent menses, infertility, low estrogen, and elevated FSH.
